description: ctadl query model for the TaintBench `cajino_baidu` app. Sources and sinks are
derived from the framework methods named in the source/sink IR (Jimple) signatures
of cajino_baidu_findings.json. Sources: File.listFiles() lists the files to leak;
Cursor.getString() reads contact/SMS columns; LocationManager.getLastKnownLocation()
reads location; TelephonyManager.getDeviceId() reads the IMEI; File.<init>(String)
names a file whose path is then leaked. Sinks: BaiduBCS.putObject() uploads to Baidu
cloud storage; FileWriter.write() writes the data to a local file; File.delete()
deletes a (tainted) file. Sinks use Argument(*) so any tainted argument reaching the
call is a leak; File.delete()/File.<init> use Argument(0) (the receiver / first arg).
putObject(PutObjectRequest) takes a request object rather than the raw data, and the
exfiltrated value is stored in the request's `object` (upload-key) field (e.g. finding
#7, where the device id becomes the upload key). ctadl is field-sensitive, so a sink
on the bare argument does not fire on a tainted subfield; the second putObject sink
names that field explicitly, matched by its full IR field descriptor (not short name).
File.listFiles() returns a File[], and the flows read elements out of it
(`files[i].toString()`). The dex frontend models an array access as the field `[]`, so an
element sits at the access path `.\[]` -- a strictly longer sibling of the empty path the
Return source is seeded at, which precise path-matched propagation will not follow. The
source is therefore marked `saturating`, so reading any offset/element off the returned
array is tainted. This is the same situation as C's `argv` in docs/model-generators.md.
ctadl ignores the non-schema `description` key, as it does `expected_lines` in the
nightly models.
